A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cyclic-consistency defense for MRI reconstruction. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, allowing retained content to be matched despite extensive reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original fastMRI reconstruction experiments, including PSNR/SSIM comparisons, adaptive attacks, detection analyses and reconstruction-stage ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds a sparse k-space perturbation experiment illustrating herringbone artifacts and their mitigation.

M1.justification: Equation (10), Algorithm 1, network architectures and blind parameter-search procedure are retained. The new sparse attack supplies an evaluation scenario without changing the defense. The correction from argmin to min in the adaptive-loss definition matches the objective already described in v2, without establishing an implementation change.

E1.justification: The fastMRI Cor-PD knee and Ax-FLAIR brain coverage is retained. v3 adds a distinct input-corruption scenario involving sparse, bounded k-space spikes that simulate herringbone artifacts (Section 4.2 and Appendix B).

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain MoDL, adversarial training, SMUG and the same alternative training formulation and reconstruction networks. The new herringbone example compares against the already-used MoDL baseline; added citations do not introduce evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Appendix B introduces a protocol for the herringbone test: 25 spike locations sampled preferentially at low frequencies, amplitudes bounded by 0.06 times the maximum measurement value, and 10 PGD iterations. Previously reported acquisition, attack and adaptive-evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new herringbone case tests whether small sparse measurement spikes destabilize reconstruction and whether mitigation removes their artifacts. Detection analyses, clean-input behavior, adaptive-attack checks and the reconstruction-stage ablation already appear in v2 and are retained.

E5.justification: Population metrics and Figure 7's violin distributions, medians and quartiles retain their reporting practices. Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests that are added or revised in the other.

E6.justification: The known/blind image-domain attack PSNR entries change from 33.23/32.94 in v2 Table 8 to 35.14/34.72 in v3 Table 10, whose caption now specifies Cor-PD. Figures 2 and 9 also revise brain examples and scores. New Figure 5 reports herringbone-example PSNR/SSIM of 37.19/0.950 after mitigation versus MoDL's 33.94/0.914. Most existing results are unchanged; these revisions do not establish same-setting performance gains between versions.

T1.justification: v2 provides an intuitive attack-propagation explanation without a theorem. v3 adds Theorem 1 and Appendix G's smooth-coil assumptions, lemmas, corollary and error-propagation proof bounding reconstruction differences on acquired measurements. It also corrects the adaptive objective's g definition from an argmin to a scalar minimum.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion add the claimed first realistic sparse-and-bounded MRI attack scenario linked to herringbone artifacts, together with mitigation in that setting. The principal training-free, blind, architecture-general and adaptive-robustness claims are retained.

C2.justification: Section 2.4 and Appendix B add a concrete interpretation connecting hardware-related impulses to herringbone artifacts and arguing that spikes invisible in input images can destabilize DL reconstruction. They also explain how spike frequency affects artifact appearance. Existing applicability discussions and adaptive-attack interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B supplies spike-selection and optimization details for the new experiment. Conversely, v2 Section 4.2's explicit statement and denominator for normalizing the implemented cyclic loss disappear from v3. Blind schedules, checkpointing and fixed-noise disclosures are retained through relocation.

R1.justification: v3 adds artifact references such as Stadler et al. and Jin et al., and theoretical context including Pramanik et al. and Uecker et al.; several general MRI background references are removed. The realistic-attack positioning expands, while the relationship to cyclic-consistency methods and existing defenses remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, affiliation/contact text, abstract and several paragraphs are edited or condensed. Dataset details merge into implementation details, and blind/adaptive material is regrouped in appendices. The overall background-method-experiments-conclusion narrative remains recognizable.

P2.justification: The document changes throughout from two-column to single-column formatting, with resized and repositioned figures, tables and algorithms. v3 adds herringbone Figure 5, moves the former blind-mitigation Figure 5 to Appendix E as Figure 12, and rearranges the non-uniform reconstruction comparison into a horizontal display. Table numbering also becomes continuous.

improvement.justification: v3 adds a useful, explicitly specified herringbone example and corrects the scalar adaptive-loss definition. However, Appendix G's Corollary 1.1 claims a small unsampled-encoding-operator norm from coil smoothness; constant normalized coil maps satisfy its stated smoothness condition while that operator has norm 1 when frequencies are omitted. This compromises the new theoretical justification. Together with the lost loss-normalization disclosure, these rigor and reproducibility concerns prevent a reliable net quality judgment despite the added empirical coverage.
